Lead paint: the short version for Dolton

Assume there is old paint under the current coat. On 1960s housing, which is most of Dolton, that is the safe assumption, and paint from before 1978 can be leaded. It affects the setup of a Dolton job at both ends, the sealing off before and the cleanup after, and not much in between.

The rule does not say a Dolton house cannot be painted. It says how the area gets sealed off, how the dust is contained and how the site is left. The trigger in a 1965-median room is about six square feet of disturbed paint, twenty outside, and any window replacement or demolition at all.

None of it is graded at the town line. The rule attaches to a build year and to the work being done, so the number worth checking is the one on your own deed in Dolton.

The Census publishes a pre-1980 bucket rather than a pre-1978 one, and on that measure 86.4 percent of the housing sits on the older side of the line in Dolton. Housing that old falls under the federal Renovation, Repair and Painting rule, which covers any work disturbing paint in a home built before 1978. Illinois is not an authorized state for it, so EPA runs it here directly.

Ask about it early. It changes the sequence of a job rather than the price of the paint, and a contractor who has thought about it will tell you in plain terms what happens on day one.

Why two quotes for the same Dolton house come out different

Aluminum and steel are the surprise on 1965-era houses: soffit, fascia wrap, gutters and often the garage door. They take paint perfectly well and they take it badly if nobody cleans the chalk off first. On the 79.7 percent of Dolton that is detached houses, that one step is the difference between an exterior that lasts and one that comes off in sheets. The 5,700 to 2,219 split between owning and renting in Dolton means the same street can want two different things. A contractor who prices both the same way is wrong about one of them.
